lessonTitle: Liver Disease: Liver Function Patterns, Cirrhosis and Jaundice

blocks.text: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis arrives with a swollen abdomen, fever and new drowsiness. Overnight his blood tests are unremarkable except for a bilirubin of 60 micromol/L and an INR of 1.9. The liver does an extraordinary amount of work, and each of its failures leaves a recognisable signature in the blood tests and on the examination.

blocks.markdown: The liver receives blood from the hepatic artery and, mainly, the portal vein. Hepatocytes synthesise albumin and clotting factors, conjugate and excrete **bilirubin** into bile, metabolise drugs, and convert ammonia to urea. Bile drains through canaliculi and the biliary tree to the duodenum. Liver injury therefore shows up as **hepatocellular** damage (enzymes released from injured hepatocytes: **ALT** and **AST**) or **cholestasis** (obstructed or impaired bile flow: **ALP** and **GGT**, with conjugated bilirubin). Synthetic function is assessed by **albumin** and **prothrombin time (INR)**, which are the true measures of liver function; transaminases are markers of injury only.

blocks.title: The R ratio
blocks.text: To classify a liver enzyme pattern, divide the ALT by its upper limit of normal (ULN) by the ALP divided by its ULN. R above 5 is hepatocellular, below 2 is cholestatic, and 2 to 5 is mixed. It is used in drug-induced liver injury and in clinical practice for a quick pattern.

blocks.caption: R ratio for pattern of liver injury.

blocks.title: Hepatocellular or cholestatic?
blocks.prompt: A patient's ALT is 600 U/L (ULN 40) and ALP is 150 U/L (ULN 120). Calculate R and classify.

steps.text: ALT as a multiple of ULN.
ALP as a multiple of ULN.
R above 5 indicates a hepatocellular pattern, so look for viral hepatitis, drugs and toxins (including paracetamol), alcohol, autoimmune and ischaemic causes.

rows: Unconjugated; no bilirubin in urine; normal stool colour
Hepatocyte damage impairs uptake, conjugation and excretion
Viral hepatitis, alcohol, drug injury, cirrhosis
Conjugated; dark urine, pale stools, pruritus; high ALP and GGT
Gallstone in common bile duct, pancreatic head cancer, cholangiocarcinoma
blocks.caption: Evaluation of jaundice.

blocks.markdown: **Evaluating jaundice.** History: pain, fever, weight loss, drugs and alcohol, travel, injection or sexual risk, family history, pale stools and dark urine, pruritus. Examination: stigmata of chronic liver disease, hepatomegaly, a palpable gallbladder (painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder suggests pancreatic head cancer), signs of malignancy. Tests: fractionated bilirubin, liver enzymes, INR, albumin, full blood count and film, viral serology and an **abdominal ultrasound** to look for dilated bile ducts. **Main causes of acute liver injury** include viral hepatitis (A, B, E), paracetamol overdose, other drugs and herbal products, alcohol, ischaemic hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis and Wilson disease. In paracetamol overdose the antidote is **N-acetylcysteine**, which should be started promptly according to the treatment nomogram and local guidance.

**Cirrhosis** is diffuse fibrosis with nodule formation, from chronic injury (alcohol, viral hepatitis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and others). Fibrosis raises resistance to portal flow, causing **portal hypertension**, and the failing liver reduces synthesis and detoxification. **Ascites** forms from portal hypertension, splanchnic vasodilation, sodium retention and low albumin. The serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) separates portal hypertensive causes (SAAG 11 g/L or more) from others. Treatment is dietary sodium restriction, spironolactone (with or without furosemide), and therapeutic paracentesis with albumin for tense ascites. **Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)** is infected ascites without a surgical source, diagnosed by an ascitic neutrophil count of 250 cells/mm3 or more and treated with intravenous antibiotics (and albumin); every patient with ascites admitted to hospital needs a diagnostic paracentesis.

blocks.caption: SAAG in g/L; 11 g/L or more indicates portal hypertension.

blocks.title: Interpreting ascites
blocks.prompt: A patient has serum albumin 30 g/L and ascitic albumin 22 g/L. Calculate the SAAG and interpret it.

steps.text: 8 g/L is below 11 g/L, so the ascites is not due to portal hypertension.
Think of peritoneal causes such as malignancy or tuberculosis, or protein-losing states such as nephrotic syndrome. Cell count, cytology and culture are needed.

blocks.answer: SAAG 8 g/L: low gradient, non-portal-hypertensive ascites.

items: Varices: portal hypertension opens collaterals at the lower oesophagus and gastric fundus. Primary prevention is a non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol or carvedilol) or endoscopic band ligation.
Acute variceal bleed: resuscitation, terlipressin, prophylactic antibiotics, urgent endoscopy with band ligation; TIPSS if refractory.

Hepatic encephalopathy: confusion, day-night reversal, asterixis, from ammonia and other gut-derived toxins that bypass the failing liver. Look for precipitants (infection, GI bleeding, constipation, sedatives, electrolyte disturbance).
Treat encephalopathy with lactulose to produce 2 to 3 soft stools a day, and rifaximin to prevent recurrence; treat the precipitant.
Other complications: hepatorenal syndrome, hepatocellular carcinoma (surveillance by ultrasound), coagulopathy.

blocks.title: Sedatives and cirrhosis
blocks.text: Benzodiazepines and opioids can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy and are used cautiously, if at all. Always consider SBP and bleeding in a cirrhotic patient who becomes drowsy.

points: ALT and AST rise in hepatocellular injury; ALP, GGT and conjugated bilirubin rise in cholestasis; albumin and INR reflect synthetic function.
Jaundice is pre-hepatic, hepatic or post-hepatic; ultrasound looks for duct dilation.
Causes of acute liver injury include viral hepatitis, paracetamol, other drugs, alcohol and ischaemia.
Cirrhosis causes portal hypertension (ascites, varices, SBP) and failure of detoxification (encephalopathy).

questions.stem: A 31-year-old has ALT 900 U/L, AST 700 U/L, ALP 110 U/L (ULN 130) and bilirubin 40 micromol/L after a week of malaise and dark urine. Which pattern of injury is this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: transaminases are far above the ALP.
distractorRationale.b: A cholestatic pattern has a disproportionately raised ALP.
distractorRationale.c: Pre-hepatic jaundice has normal liver enzymes.

questions.explanation: A marked rise in ALT and AST with a normal ALP shows hepatocyte injury, as in viral or drug-induced hepatitis. R would be well above 5.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man has painless jaundice, weight loss, dark urine, pale stools and pruritus. ALP is 520 U/L (ULN 130), GGT is raised and ALT 80 U/L (ULN 40). What is the most appropriate first investigation?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: look for biliary dilation in obstructive jaundice.
distractorRationale.b: Viral hepatitis gives a hepatocellular pattern.
distractorRationale.c: AMA is for primary biliary cholangitis, a later step.
distractorRationale.d: Biopsy is not first-line for obstructive jaundice.

questions.explanation: A cholestatic pattern with dark urine, pale stools and pruritus suggests biliary obstruction, and ultrasound is a quick, non-invasive test for duct dilation. Painless jaundice with weight loss raises concern for malignancy of the pancreatic head or bile duct.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old with cirrhosis becomes confused with day-night reversal and asterixis, two days after a large black stool. What is the first-line medical treatment for his encephalopathy?

options.text: Lactulose, with treatment of the precipitant

questions.correctOptionText: Lactulose, with treatment of the precipitant

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lactulose lowers gut ammonia absorption.
distractorRationale.c: Protein restriction is not advised long-term but protein loading is not a treatment.

questions.explanation: Hepatic encephalopathy results from ammonia and other toxins that bypass the failing liver. A GI bleed is a classic precipitant since digested blood adds an ammonia load, so the bleed must be treated alongside lactulose.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old with cirrhosis presents with haematemesis and hypotension. Endoscopy is planned. Which additional treatments should be given alongside resuscitation?

options.text: Terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics, then band ligation

questions.correctOptionText: Terlipressin and prophylactic antibiotics, then band ligation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: standard acute variceal bleed care.
distractorRationale.b: Beta-blockers can worsen hypotension in an acute bleed.

questions.explanation: Terlipressin reduces portal pressure, antibiotics reduce infection and mortality in cirrhotic bleeds, and band ligation at endoscopy controls the varix. Non-selective beta-blockers are used for prevention, not as acute treatment.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old presents 10 hours after intentionally ingesting 30 g of paracetamol. He is currently well. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start intravenous N-acetylcysteine promptly, guided by local guidance and paracetamol level

questions.correctOptionText: Start intravenous N-acetylcysteine promptly, guided by local guidance and paracetamol level

distractorRationale.a: Correct: N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and prevents liver injury, and is most effective if given early.
distractorRationale.b: Patients are asymptomatic for hours despite later severe injury.
distractorRationale.c: Lactulose treats encephalopathy and is not an antidote.
distractorRationale.d: Vitamin K does not treat paracetamol toxicity.

questions.explanation: Paracetamol overdose produces a toxic metabolite that depletes glutathione and injures hepatocytes, usually without symptoms early on. N-acetylcysteine acts as a glutathione precursor and is lifesaving when started early.

questions.stem: A patient has ALT 480 U/L (ULN 40) and ALP 180 U/L (ULN 120). Calculate the R ratio (unitless).
questions.explanation: ALT is 480 / 40 = 12 times ULN and ALP is 180 / 120 = 1.5 times ULN, so R = 12 / 1.5 = 8. This is above 5, indicating a hepatocellular pattern.

questions.stem: A patient with ascites has serum albumin 27 g/L and ascitic fluid albumin 5 g/L. Calculate the serum-ascites albumin gradient in g/L.
questions.explanation: SAAG = 27 - 5 = 22 g/L. A gradient of 11 g/L or more indicates portal hypertension, consistent with cirrhosis, and the ascites should also be sampled for neutrophil count to exclude SBP.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with alcohol-related cirrhosis is admitted with abdominal distension and diffuse tenderness but no drowsiness. Describe how you would investigate the ascites, how you would diagnose spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and the principles of managing ascites.
markingGuide: Diagnostic paracentesis in every patient admitted with ascites
Ascitic fluid cell count and neutrophil count, culture, albumin and total protein
SBP: ascitic neutrophils 250 cells/mm3 or more
SAAG 11 g/L or more indicates portal hypertension
SBP treated with intravenous antibiotics, and albumin infusion
Ascites: sodium restriction, spironolactone with or without furosemide
Therapeutic paracentesis with albumin for tense ascites
Mechanism: portal hypertension, vasodilation, sodium retention, hypoalbuminaemia
questions.explanation: Diagnostic paracentesis detects infected ascites, which is common and lethal if missed in cirrhosis. Management combines diuretic and sodium restriction with large-volume paracentesis and albumin when ascites is tense.

questions.stem: Outline your approach to evaluating a patient presenting with jaundice, and list the main causes of acute liver injury.
markingGuide: Classify as pre-hepatic, hepatic or post-hepatic
History: pain, fever, weight loss, pruritus, dark urine, pale stools, drugs, alcohol, travel, risk factors
Examination: stigmata of chronic liver disease, hepatomegaly, palpable gallbladder
Tests: fractionated bilirubin, liver enzymes, INR, albumin, FBC, viral serology
Causes of acute liver injury: viral hepatitis A, B, E; paracetamol and other drugs; alcohol; ischaemia; autoimmune hepatitis; Wilson disease
questions.explanation: Classifying jaundice by mechanism directs investigation, and an enzyme pattern together with ultrasound separates obstructive from hepatocellular causes. Acute liver injury must be recognised early, especially paracetamol toxicity, which has a specific antidote.

questions.stem: True or false: a patient with cirrhosis and ascites who is admitted to hospital should have a diagnostic paracentesis to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
questions.explanation: SBP can be clinically subtle and carries a high mortality if untreated, so ascitic fluid is sampled on admission. A neutrophil count of 250 cells/mm3 or more confirms it.
